messages.subject: Hierarchical modeling joined response and response times.
parts:
Hi Ratan's users,

I'm writing to make sure that my code I write reflects the hierarchical model defined below.
  1. To first level, Responses are defined with ranch model and log response times to normal distribution
  2. To second level, parameters of persons are multivariate normal distribution. Also parameters of items.

If applicable, what is the best way to write the priors for variances covariances matrix and mu because I doubt of this in my code.

data {

  int P; // # Individus

  int Q; // # Items

  real logTwNA[P,Q]; // Log responses times

  real IndwNA[P,Q]; // NA index  (1 if NA, 0 ifelse)

  int RwNA[P,Q]; // Responses

}


parameters {

vector[2] paramP[P]; // Parameters of persons (theta,tau)

vector[2] paramQ[Q]; // Parameters of items (betaR,betaT)


        // Parameters's distributions of parameters of persons

  vector[2] muP;

  corr_matrix[2] rhoP;

  vector<lower=0,upper=100>[2] sigmaP;

  

        // Parameters's distributions of parameters of items

  vector[2] muQ;

  corr_matrix[2] rhoQ;

  vector<lower=0,upper=100>[2] sigmaQ;

  

        // Sd of log response time of each item 

  vector<lower=0,upper=100>[Q] sigmaT;

}


transformed parameters {

cov_matrix[2] omegaP;

cov_matrix[2] omegaQ;

        // Covariance matrix defined for parameters of persons

for(i in 1:2)

{

omegaP[i,i] <- sigmaP[i]*sigmaP[i]*rhoP[i,i];

}

omegaP[1,2] <- sigmaP[1]*sigmaP[2]*rhoP[1,2];

omegaP[2,1] <- omegaP[1,2];

        // Covariance matrix defined for parameters of items

for(i in 1:2)

{

omegaQ[i,i] <- sigmaQ[i]*sigmaQ[i]*rhoQ[i,i];

}

omegaQ[1,2] <- sigmaQ[1]*sigmaQ[2]*rhoQ[1,2];

omegaQ[2,1] <- omegaQ[1,2];

}


model {

  

  // Priors omegaP ~ inversewishart(2,matrix(c(1,0,0,1,ncol=2)), omegaQ ~ inversewishart(2,matrix(c(10,1,1,10,ncol=2))

  // muP ~ MVN(c(0,0),omegaP), muQ ~ MVN(c(0,0),omegaQ)


  matrix[2,2] omegaQ0;

  vector[2] muP0;

  vector[2] muQ0;

  

  muP0 <- rep_vector(0,2);

  mu00 <- rep_vector(0,2);


  omegaQ0 <- diag_matrix(rep_vector(10,2));

  omegaQ0[1,2] <- 1;

  omegaQ0[2,1] <- 1;

  

  omegaP ~ inv_wishart(2,diag_matrix(rep_vector(1,2)));

  omegaQ ~ inv_wishart(2,omegaQ0);

  

  muP ~ multi_normal(muP0,omegaP);

  muQ ~ multi_normal(muQ0,omegaQ);

    

  // 1st level

  for(p in 1:P)

  {

    for(q in 1:Q)

    {

      if(IndwNA[p,q]==0)

      {

        RwNA[p,q] ~ bernoulli_logit(paramP[p,1]-paramQ[q,1]);

        logTwNA[p,q] ~ normal(paramQ[q,2] - paramP[p,2],sigmaT[q]);

      }

    }

  }

  

  // 2nd level

  for(p in 1:P)

  {

    paramP[p] ~ multi_normal(muP,omegaP);

  }

  

  for(q in 1:Q)

  {

    paramQ[q] ~ multi_normal(muQ,omegaQ);

  }

}


Thank you to understand me, because I try to have even more insurance in the writing Bayesian method with Rstan.

Bests regards.
Eric I. E.

So if you literally want to do what R's doing in
terms of broadcasting (filling):

matrix add_broadcast(vector x, matrix y) {
int pos;
matrix xpy[rows(y), cols(y)];
if (num_elements(x) == 0) return y;
pos <- 1;
for (n in 1:cols(y)) {
for (m in 1:rows(y)) {
if (pos > num_elements(x)) pos <- 1;
xpy[m, n] <- xpy[m, n] + x[pos];
pos <- pos + 1;
}
}
return xpy;
}

But you probably want the simpler thing of taking a column vector
and adding it to each column, which you can do with a much simpler
loop.

R's just filling column major:

       [,1] [,2] [,3]
  [1,]   11 1003  105
  [2,]  102   14 1006

So if you literally want to do what R's doing in
terms of broadcasting (filling):

  matrix add_broadcast(vector x, matrix y) {
    int pos;
    matrix xpy[rows(y), cols(y)];
    if (num_elements(x) == 0) return y;
    pos <- 1;
    for (n in 1:cols(y)) {
      for (m in 1:rows(y)) {
        if (pos > num_elements(x)) pos <- 1;
        xpy[m, n] <- xpy[m, n] + x[pos];
        pos <- pos + 1;
      }
    }
    return xpy;
  }

But you probably want the simpler thing of taking a column vector
and adding it to each column, which you can do with a much simpler
loop.

So how to define a and b to do a+b in Rstan.

Stan is stricter than R when it comes to arithmetic with matrices and vectors. R will cheat for you so that a + b is valid when a is a vector and b is a matrix, but Stan requires you to do proper matrix arithmetic. If you want to add a to each column of b you can use rep_matrix(a, 3) + b, which will make a 2x3 matrix where each column is a copy of a and then it will add that matrix to b.
